content: Candida is a normal commensal organism found on the skin and mucous membranes. A healthy immune system and intact, regenerating skin are essential to prevent Candida from becoming pathogenic. Candida Virulence Factors: 1. Candida produces molecules that allow it to adhere to host cells. 2. It secretes hydrolases, which have a lytic effect on tissues, facilitating fungal invasion. 3. Candida exhibits polymorphism, meaning it can grow in two forms: pseudohyphae (elongated ellipsoid forms) or yeast (rounded to oval budding forms). While the exact role of polymorphism in virulence is unclear, species capable of causing severe disease often exhibit this ability. 4. Candida can form biofilms, which are thick layers of fungal organisms on mucosal surfaces, catheters, or dentures. Biofilm formation increases the risk of candidiasis, especially in patients with compromised immunity or poor general health. The VPS4 gene in Candida plays a significant role in oropharyngeal candidiasis, and mutations in this gene reduce fungal virulence. Gross Pathology of Oropharyngeal Candidiasis: 1. Pseudomembranous Candidiasis: Characterized by curdy white plaques on the mucosa, which can be seen during examination. Common in newborns or immunocompromised individuals, or those using corticosteroids. 2. Atrophic Candidiasis: Presents as erythema or edema without the typical white plaques. Often seen in patients with dental dentures. 3. Chronic Hyperplastic Candidiasis (Candidal Leukoplakia): Persistent, tough, adherent white lesions that require biopsy for differentiation from other leukoplakias. More common in smokers, individuals with iron deficiency anemia, or those with impaired cell-mediated immunity. 4. Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis (CMCC): A syndrome involving chronic or recurrent superficial Candida infections of the skin and mucous membranes. Associated with endocrine and autoimmune disorders, such as hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency. Characterized by T-cell dysfunction in response to Candida antigens. Infections are usually superficial but can become invasive, particularly in newborns. Microscopic Pathology: Examination of wet mounts with 10% KOH or saline reveals hyphae, pseudohyphae, and blastospores. Clinical History and Symptoms: Oropharyngeal candidiasis can be asymptomatic, especially in mild cases or in patients with poor general health. Symptoms may include dysphagia, odynophagia, white patches on the mouth and tongue (in pseudomembranous candidiasis), difficulty tasting food, and a sensation of fullness or discomfort in the mouth. Thrush and Breastfeeding: The increased use of antibiotics during labor to prevent Group B streptococcal transmission has led to a rise in thrush cases. Symptoms in infants include oral rashes and persistent diaper rashes unresponsive to conventional treatments. Breastfeeding mothers may experience burning and painful nipples, which can range from mild to severe, complicating breastfeeding. Over-the-counter antifungal creams (7-day formulations) can be applied to the affected areas, with improvement typically seen within 24–48 hours. Creams should be washed off the nipples before breastfeeding. Physical Examination Findings: 1. Pseudomembranous Oropharyngeal Candidiasis: White plaques on the mouth and tongue. Attempting to remove the plaques with a tongue depressor leaves an erythematous area, sometimes with bleeding, distinguishing it from lichen planus. 2. Atrophic Oropharyngeal Candidiasis (Denture Stomatitis): Erythematous lesions without white plaques. Lesions are typically located where dentures make contact with the mucosa. 3. Hyperplastic Oropharyngeal Candidiasis (Candidal Leukoplakia): Rough, irregular, nodular white plaques on an erythematous base, often on the buccal mucosa or tongue. Non-homogeneous (speckled) leukoplakias are common. 4. Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis: Recurrent or persistent Candida infections affecting the mouth, tongue, scalp, and nails. Chronic infections can lead to disfigurement and thickening of affected areas. Nails may appear brittle and broken. Rarely, systemic candidiasis may develop, especially in the presence of other immunodeficiencies. Autoimmune disorders such as hypoparathyroidism, diabetes mellitus, or Grave’s disease are often associated. Laboratory Findings: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, with confirmatory tests rarely required. Oral smears are obtained by gently scraping lesions and spreading the material on a glass slide. In hyperplastic candidiasis, a biopsy is indicated. Smears and biopsies can be stained with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain, which highlights fungal walls in red. Candida can also be identified using Gram stain, as it is strongly Gram-positive. Histopathologic Examination: 1. Pseudomembranous Candidiasis: The epithelium appears thickened with parakeratosis (superficial separation of epithelial layers). Polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) infiltrate the epithelium, while chronic inflammatory cells infiltrate the lamina propria. Pseudohyphae are seen as weakly basophilic structures embedded in the epithelium. 2. Atrophic Candidiasis: Similar to pseudomembranous candidiasis but lacks parakeratosis. The epithelium is atrophic and thin. 3. Hyperplastic Candidiasis: The epithelium is hyperplastic, hyperkeratotic, and acanthotic, with dysplasia in some cases. Causes of Oropharyngeal Candidiasis: 1. Most Common Cause: Candida albicans. 2. Less Common Causes: Candida krusei. Candida glabrata. Candida tropicalis.
